ecg-cond-042.question: QRS 130 ms, rSR' pattern in V1, broad slurred S wave in leads I and V6. What is the diagnosis?
commentaires: Correct: QRS ≥ 120 ms, rSR' in V1 and a broad S wave in I/V6 reflect delayed RV activation.
Incorrect: LBBB produces a QS or rS pattern in V1 and broad notched R waves in I and V6.
Incorrect: isolated fascicular block does not widen the QRS to 130 ms or produce rSR' in V1.
Incorrect: there is no short PR interval or delta wave in this description.
ecg-cond-042.explication: Complete RBBB combines a QRS ≥ 120 ms, an rsr', rsR' or rSR' pattern in V1–V2 (R' usually taller than r) and a broad S wave (> 40 ms or longer than the R wave) in leads I and V6. These abnormalities reflect delayed activation of the right ventricle. LBBB, by contrast, produces broad notched or slurred R waves in I, aVL and V5–V6, with QS or rS in V1. Left anterior fascicular block does not on its own produce a QRS ≥ 120 ms. Pre-excitation combines a short PR interval and a delta wave.
ecg-cond-042.aRetenir: RBBB: rSR' in V1 and broad S in I/V6, QRS ≥ 120 ms.

ecg-cond-043.question: Which criterion is part of the definition of complete left bundle branch block (AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009)?
options: Notched R in V5–V6 with a small septal q wave preserved
Broad notched R in I, aVL, V5–V6, with no septal q wave
rSR' pattern in V1 with a broad S wave in I and V6
QRS between 100 and 110 ms with a QS pattern in V1
commentaires: Incorrect: a persistent lateral septal q wave should cast doubt on true LBBB.
Correct: reversed septal activation (loss of the lateral q wave) and broad notched R waves in the left-sided leads.
Incorrect: this is the right bundle branch block pattern.
Incorrect: complete LBBB requires a QRS ≥ 120 ms in adults.
ecg-cond-043.explication: In LBBB, septal depolarisation occurs from right to left: the physiological septal q wave disappears in I, V5 and V6, and the R waves are broad, notched or slurred in the lateral leads. V1 shows a QS or rS pattern. QRS duration must be ≥ 120 ms in adults. The rSR' pattern in V1 is that of RBBB. A persistent lateral septal q wave should cast doubt on the diagnosis (non-specific conduction delay, old infarction).
ecg-cond-043.aRetenir: LBBB: QRS ≥ 120 ms, broad notched lateral R waves, no septal q wave in I/V5/V6.

ecg-cond-044.question: Which criteria are part of the definition of left anterior fascicular block according to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations?
options: rS pattern in II, III and aVF
qR pattern in III and aVF
commentaires: Correct: left axis deviation between −45° and −90°; between −30° and −45°, the criterion is not met.
Correct: qR pattern in aVL, with a delayed R-wave peak time.
Correct: activation starts in the inferoposterior region, hence an rS pattern in the inferior leads.
Incorrect: isolated fascicular block has a QRS < 120 ms; beyond that, a bundle branch block is associated.
Incorrect: qR in III and aVF belongs to left posterior fascicular block.
ecg-cond-044.explication: Left anterior fascicular block is the most common fascicular conduction disorder: activation starts in the inferoposterior region and then spreads upwards and to the left. It combines left axis deviation between −45° and −90°, a qR pattern in aVL (with delayed R-wave peak time), an rS pattern in II, III and aVF, and a QRS < 120 ms: a QRS ≥ 120 ms suggests an associated bundle branch block. The qR pattern in III and aVF belongs to left posterior fascicular block. An axis between −30° and −45° is not sufficient according to the 2009 AHA criteria and warrants a search for another cause.
ecg-cond-044.aRetenir: LAFB: axis −45° to −90°, qR in aVL, rS in the inferior leads, QRS < 120 ms.

ecg-cond-045.question: ECG: axis +120°, rS pattern in I and aVL, qR in III and aVF, QRS 100 ms. Before diagnosing left posterior fascicular block, which diagnosis must be excluded first?
options: Old inferior infarction (q waves in III, aVF)
Acute pericarditis in its early phase
commentaires: Incorrect: inferior infarction rather shifts the axis to the left; it is extensive lateral infarction that must be excluded.
Incorrect: the QRS measures 100 ms and nothing suggests peaked T waves; this is not the picture.
Correct: LPFB is a diagnosis of exclusion; right ventricular overload is the first cause of right axis deviation to exclude.
Incorrect: pericarditis alters the ST segment and PR segment, not the QRS axis.
ecg-cond-045.explication: Left posterior fascicular block is rare, as the posterior fascicle is short, thick and has a dual blood supply. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: other causes of right axis deviation must be ruled out, in particular right ventricular hypertrophy or overload, a slender body habitus, extensive lateral infarction and pulmonary embolism. The AHA criteria combine an axis of +90° to +180°, rS in I and aVL, qR in III and aVF and a QRS < 120 ms. Combined with RBBB, it forms bifascicular block with a poor prognosis. Inferior infarction, by contrast, shifts the axis to the left, and neither hyperkalaemia nor pericarditis produces this picture with a QRS of 100 ms.
ecg-cond-045.aRetenir: LPFB = diagnosis of exclusion: rule out right ventricular overload or a slender body habitus.

ecg-cond-046.question: In an adult, a QRS of 115 ms with an rsR' pattern in V1 and a broad S wave in I and V6 corresponds to complete right bundle branch block.
commentaires: Incorrect: the morphology is that of RBBB, but a QRS of 115 ms defines incomplete block; complete block requires ≥ 120 ms.
Correct: RBBB morphology with a QRS between 110 and 119 ms = incomplete RBBB (AHA/ACCF/HRS 2009).
ecg-cond-046.explication: False. According to the 2009 AHA/ACCF/HRS recommendations, an RBBB morphology (rsR' in V1–V2, broad S in I and V6) with a QRS between 110 and 119 ms in an adult defines incomplete RBBB. Complete RBBB requires a QRS ≥ 120 ms. An rSr' pattern with a QRS < 110 ms is often a normal variant, common in young people and athletes. Incomplete RBBB should nevertheless raise the possibility of an atrial septal defect or, with ST elevation in V1–V2, Brugada syndrome.
ecg-cond-046.aRetenir: RBBB: incomplete if QRS 110–119 ms, complete from 120 ms in adults.

ecg-cond-047.question: Which criteria belong to Strauss's strict definition of left bundle branch block, used to predict response to cardiac resynchronisation?
options: QRS ≥ 140 ms in men or ≥ 130 ms in women
QS or rS pattern in V1 and V2
Mid-QRS notching required in all six leads V1, V2, V5, V6, I and aVL
Presence of a septal q wave in V6
commentaires: Correct: a higher duration threshold than the classic definition, differing by sex.
Correct: QS or rS pattern in V1 and V2, reflecting activation moving away from the RV.
Incorrect: mid-QRS notching is required in at least two of these leads, not all six.
Incorrect: a septal q wave in V6 is incompatible with true LBBB.
Incorrect: the axis is not part of the Strauss definition.
ecg-cond-047.explication: Strauss et al. (2011) proposed strict criteria because about a third of "conventional" LBBB actually corresponds to LV hypertrophy combined with non-specific conduction delay. True LBBB requires a QRS ≥ 140 ms (men) or ≥ 130 ms (women), a QS or rS pattern in V1–V2, and mid-QRS notching in at least two of V1, V2, V5, V6, I and aVL: it is not required in all of them. A septal q wave in V6 is incompatible with true LBBB. The axis is not part of the definition. These criteria identify the patients who respond best to CRT.
ecg-cond-047.aRetenir: Strauss LBBB: QRS ≥ 140/130 ms, QS/rS in V1–V2, mid-QRS notching in ≥ 2 leads.

ecg-cond-048.question: With a broad QRS (≥ 120 ms) of supraventricular origin, how can you quickly distinguish RBBB from LBBB by looking at V1?
ecg-cond-048.reponseAttendue: In V1: a predominantly positive QRS with an rsR'/rSR' ("M") pattern = RBBB; a predominantly negative QRS (QS or rS) = LBBB. Confirm in the lateral leads: broad S in I/V6 for RBBB, broad notched R with no q wave in I/V6 for LBBB.
ecg-cond-048.explication: V1 faces the right ventricle. In RBBB, the RV is activated late, producing a positive terminal wave (R') in V1. In LBBB, delayed LV activation moves away from V1, which is therefore negative (QS or rS). The lateral leads confirm: a broad terminal S wave in I and V6 for RBBB, a broad notched R wave with no septal q wave for LBBB. Bear in mind that a broad QRS may also be VT, pre-excitation or a paced rhythm.
ecg-cond-048.aRetenir: Terminal positivity in V1 = RBBB; negative V1 = LBBB.

ecg-cond-049.question: Which combination defines bifascicular block?
options: First-degree AV block + left anterior fascicular block
Incomplete RBBB + associated first-degree AV block
Two consecutive blocked P waves (3:1 AV block)
RBBB combined with left fascicular block
commentaires: Incorrect: first-degree AV block is not a fascicular block; it may be nodal.
Incorrect: neither incomplete RBBB nor a long PR interval defines disease of two fascicles.
Incorrect: two consecutive blocked P waves define high-grade AV block, not fascicular block.
Correct: disease of two of the three fascicles, RBBB + LAFB (common) or RBBB + LPFB (rarer, more serious).
ecg-cond-049.explication: The intraventricular conduction system classically comprises three fascicles: the right bundle branch, the left anterior fascicle and the left posterior fascicle. Bifascicular block involves two of them: RBBB + LAFB (the most common) or RBBB + LPFB (rarer, more serious). Complete LBBB is sometimes considered bifascicular. First-degree AV block is not a fascicular block: it may be nodal. Two consecutive blocked P waves define high-grade AV block.
ecg-cond-049.aRetenir: Bifascicular block = RBBB + LAFB or RBBB + LPFB.

ecg-cond-050.question: The term "trifascicular block" applied to the combination of RBBB + LAFB + first-degree AV block is a misnomer, because the PR prolongation may be nodal in origin.
commentaires: Correct: a long PR interval may result from a prolonged AH (nodal) with a normal HV; only the HV localises the delay.
Incorrect: the statement is true; the true ECG equivalent of trifascicular block is alternating bundle branch block.
ecg-cond-050.explication: True. PR prolongation in bifascicular block may reflect nodal delay (prolonged AH interval) with a normal HV interval, rather than disease of the third fascicle. Only measurement of the HV interval at electrophysiological study can localise the delay. Guidelines therefore prefer to describe the combination (bifascicular block with first-degree AV block). The true ECG equivalent of trifascicular block is alternating bundle branch block, which is a class I indication for pacing.
ecg-cond-050.aRetenir: RBBB + LAFB + long PR is not necessarily trifascicular: only the HV interval localises the delay.

ecg-cond-051.question: A 70-year-old asymptomatic patient is found incidentally to have RBBB + LAFB with a PR interval of 180 ms. According to the 2021 ESC guidelines, what is the pacing indication?
commentaires: Correct: the annual risk of complete AV block is low; follow-up and advice about symptoms are sufficient.
Incorrect: class I applies to Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block and alternating block, not this asymptomatic block.
Incorrect: no class IIa recommendation covers asymptomatic bifascicular block with a normal PR interval.
Incorrect: no heart disease with a high risk of ventricular arrhythmia is described; an ICD has no role.
ecg-cond-051.explication: The 2021 ESC guidelines do not recommend pacing (class III) in asymptomatic patients with bundle branch block or bifascicular block. The annual risk of progression to complete AV block is low. Clinical and ECG follow-up is sufficient, with advice to the patient about symptoms that should prompt review (syncope, presyncope). Assessment of LV function is useful, as bundle branch block may reveal underlying heart disease. An ICD has no role in the absence of high-risk heart disease.
ecg-cond-051.aRetenir: Asymptomatic bifascicular block: no pacing (class III).

ecg-cond-052.question: A 72-year-old man has unexplained syncope without prodrome, RBBB + LAFB, LVEF 60%, and a non-diagnostic initial work-up. What is the next step recommended by the 2021 ESC guidelines?
options: Tilt testing as the first-line investigation
EP study, with pacing if HV ≥ 70 ms or infra-Hisian block
Observation, as bifascicular block is not the cause
commentaires: Incorrect: empirical pacing is only a IIb option in elderly, frail patients.
Incorrect: tilt testing assesses reflex syncope, not His–Purkinje conduction.
Correct: pacing (class I) if HV ≥ 70 ms or induced infra-Hisian AV block; if the EP study is negative, an ILR.
Incorrect: syncope with bifascicular block raises concern for paroxysmal AV block; investigation is mandatory.
ecg-cond-052.explication: In a patient with unexplained syncope and bifascicular block, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend an electrophysiological study: an HV interval ≥ 70 ms, or second- or third-degree infra-Hisian AV block during incremental atrial pacing or pharmacological challenge (ajmaline, procainamide…), leads to a class I pacing indication. If the EP study is negative, an implantable loop recorder can document any paroxysmal AV block. Empirical pacing without an EP study is only a class IIb option in elderly, frail patients. Tilt testing does not answer the question of conduction.
ecg-cond-052.aRetenir: Syncope + bifascicular block: EP study, pacing if HV ≥ 70 ms; if negative, an implantable loop recorder.

ecg-cond-053.question: During an electrophysiological study in a patient with syncope and bifascicular block, which result leads to a class I pacing indication (ESC 2021)?
commentaires: Incorrect: a prolonged HV (normal 35–55 ms) but below the 70 ms decision threshold.
Correct: HV ≥ 70 ms in a patient with syncope and bundle branch block = class I pacing.
Incorrect: the AH interval assesses the AV node, depends on autonomic tone and is not part of the decision criterion.
Incorrect: a nodal Wenckebach point at 140 bpm reflects normal nodal conduction.
ecg-cond-053.explication: The HV interval measures conduction time through the His–Purkinje system; its normal value is about 35 to 55 ms. In a patient with syncope and bundle branch block, an HV ≥ 70 ms is considered positive and warrants class I pacing. An HV of 62 ms is prolonged but below the decision threshold. The AH interval assesses the AV node and depends heavily on autonomic tone. A nodal Wenckebach point at 140 bpm is normal. An HV ≥ 100 ms identifies a particularly high risk of complete AV block.
ecg-cond-053.aRetenir: Syncope + bundle branch block: HV ≥ 70 ms at EP study = pacing (class I).

ecg-cond-054.question: Two successive ECGs from the same patient show complete RBBB and then complete LBBB. What is the management according to the 2021 ESC guidelines?
options: Observation, since the patient is asymptomatic
24-hour Holter, pacing only if complete AV block is documented
Mandatory electrophysiological study before any decision
Pacing indicated (class I), even in the absence of symptoms
commentaires: Incorrect: the risk of sudden complete AV block is high; the absence of symptoms offers no protection.
Incorrect: waiting to document complete AV block exposes the patient to injurious syncope or sudden death.
Incorrect: an EP study is not needed; the ECG pattern is enough to establish the indication.
Correct: alternating bundle branch block is equivalent to trifascicular disease; class I pacing, with or without symptoms.
ecg-cond-054.explication: Alternating bundle branch block (RBBB and LBBB on different tracings, or RBBB alternating with LAFB then LPFB) reflects disease of all three fascicles: it is the ECG equivalent of trifascicular block, with a high risk of sudden complete AV block. The 2021 ESC guidelines recommend pacing as class I, with or without symptoms. An EP study is not needed to decide. Waiting to document complete AV block on Holter exposes the patient to injurious syncope or sudden death.
ecg-cond-054.aRetenir: Alternating bundle branch block = class I pacing, even if asymptomatic.

ecg-cond-055.question: An 86-year-old frail woman has recurrent unexplained injurious syncope, bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB) and normal LVEF. An EP study is not feasible. What do the 2021 ESC guidelines provide for?
options: Pacing contraindicated without a prior EP study
commentaires: Correct: in frail elderly patients with injurious syncope, empirical pacing may be considered (IIb).
Incorrect: the 2021 ESC guidelines specifically provide an option without an EP study in these frail patients.
Incorrect: this is not class I; in a patient who can be investigated, an EP study then an ILR remain the rule.
Incorrect: with a normal LVEF, an ICD is not an option.
ecg-cond-055.explication: In elderly, frail patients with unexplained syncope and bifascicular block and a high risk of injurious recurrence, the 2021 ESC guidelines allow empirical pacing to be considered without an EP study (class IIb). This option acknowledges that a large proportion of such syncope is due to paroxysmal AV block, while recognising that the evidence remains indirect. It is not class I: in a patient who can be investigated, an EP study followed by an implantable loop recorder remains the rule. An ICD is only discussed if LVEF is reduced.
ecg-cond-055.aRetenir: Frail elderly patient, unexplained syncope + bifascicular block: empirical pacing possible (IIb).

ecg-cond-056.question: A patient has unexplained syncope, left bundle branch block and an LVEF of 30% despite optimal medical therapy. What type of device should be discussed, and why?
ecg-cond-056.reponseAttendue: A defibrillator with resynchronisation (CRT-D) according to the heart failure guidelines, rather than a pacemaker alone: the syncope may be due to a ventricular arrhythmia rather than AV block; LBBB with LVEF ≤ 35% is also an indication for CRT.
ecg-cond-056.explication: In a patient with bundle branch block and LVEF ≤ 35%, unexplained syncope may be due to ventricular tachycardia as much as to paroxysmal AV block. In this situation, the 2021 ESC guidelines recommend considering an ICD or CRT-D according to the guidelines on heart failure and ventricular arrhythmias, rather than a pacemaker alone, which does not protect against sudden cardiac death. LBBB combined with reduced LVEF adds an indication for resynchronisation. An EP study alone is not sufficient to exclude ventricular arrhythmic risk in this setting.
ecg-cond-056.aRetenir: Syncope + bundle branch block + LVEF ≤ 35%: think ICD/CRT-D, not a pacemaker alone.
